d: From a fresh VPS to a Laravel app on HTTPS in five commands.
x: From a fresh Ubuntu server to a Laravel app on HTTPS, in about fifteen minutes. Every step shows the real command and what it prints; click a terminal to jump to the end. Install one command on the server Log in as cipi, with your SSH key Create an app isolated user, DB, PHP Deploy zero downtime from Git HTTPS Let's Encrypt, auto-renewed You need: an Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04 VPS with a public IP, a domain whose DNS you control, and a Git repository. Cipi is free; the only cost is the server. 1. Install Cipi SSH into the fresh server as root (or a sudo user) and run the installer. It asks for your

SSH into the fresh server as root (or a sudo user) and run the installer. It asks for your SSH public key, shows its plan, then installs and hardens the whole stack. $ wget -O - https://cipi.sh/setup.sh | bash Save the credentials it prints. Requirements, SSH keys and unattended installs: Install Cipi .
Root login over SSH is now off. Connect as cipi with your key and prefix commands with sudo (no password needed for cipi ). $ ssh cipi@203.0.113.10 $ sudo cipi status

The wizard asks for the app type, runtime, database, name, domain and repository, then builds an isolated app: its own Linux user, database, PHP pool, Nginx vhost, worker and deploy key. $ sudo cipi app create Skip the questions with flags: sudo cipi app create --user=myapp --domain=myapp.com \ --repository=git@github.com:you/myapp.git --branch=main The summary at the end (database password, deploy key, webhook token, a mariadb+ssh:// URL for TablePlus or DBeaver) is shown once . Save it.

If you gave the installer a Git token, there is nothing to do: Cipi added the deploy key and the push webhook to the repository. Otherwise add the ssh-ed25519 … key from the summary as a read-only deploy key : Provider Where GitHub Repository → Settings → Deploy keys GitLab Settings → Repository → Deploy keys Bitbucket Repository settings → Access keys Azure DevOps User settings → SSH public keys Then check that the server can read it: sudo cipi git check myapp . Tokens and automatic setup: Git providers .

Cipi keeps cache, sessions and queues in each app's own database , so no app can read another's data. Laravel 11+ ships those tables; on an older project create them once and commit: php artisan cache:table && php artisan session:table && php artisan queue:table Migrations run on every deploy. Prefer Valkey for speed or Horizon? Switch per app in Valkey .

$ sudo cipi deploy myapp The new release is built in its own folder, migrated, then made live with one atomic symlink swap. Visitors never see a half-deployed app, and cipi deploy myapp --rollback goes back in a second. How it works: Deploy & roll back .

Point the domain's DNS at the server, then: $ sudo cipi ssl install myapp The certificate covers the domain and its aliases and renews itself. Behind the Cloudflare proxy use --dns=cloudflare and set SSL/TLS to Full (strict) . More in SSL certificates .

Prefer a browser, or need one for clients? Install the API and the panel, each on its own domain. The panel can manage this server and any other Cipi server you connect. $ sudo cipi api api.example.com $ sudo cipi gui panel.example.com Animated clips of the web panel; see the screenshot tour .

Question Answer Can I install on a server with other software? No. Cipi needs a fresh server: it configures Nginx, PHP, users and the firewall its own way. Which size? 1 GB RAM works for a small app; 2–4 GB is comfortable for several. Where are the credentials? Printed at the end of the install, once. Save them in a password manager.

d: The stack Cipi installs and how each app is laid out on disk.
x: Cipi is a command-line tool that lives on your server. It installs a proven open-source stack, then creates and runs apps on it, each one sealed off from the others. There is no external service in the loop: no account, no agent phoning home, nothing to pay. The server Nginx web server, TLS, proxy PHP-FPM / Octane several PHP versions side by side MariaDB / PostgreSQL one database per app Valkey cache, queues (opt-in per app) Supervisor workers, Horizon, Reverb Component Role Nginx (nginx.org mainline) Web server, reverse proxy, TLS termination, HTTP/2 hardening PHP-FPM PHP runtime per app; 8.

Nginx web server, TLS, proxy PHP-FPM / Octane several PHP versions side by side MariaDB / PostgreSQL one database per app Valkey cache, queues (opt-in per app) Supervisor workers, Horizon, Reverb Component Role Nginx (nginx.org mainline) Web server, reverse proxy, TLS termination, HTTP/2 hardening PHP-FPM PHP runtime per app; 8.3 to 8.6 installable side by side Laravel Octane (FrankenPHP) Optional long-running PHP server per Laravel app MariaDB Default database; PostgreSQL optional, chosen per app Valkey Open-source Redis fork for cache, sessions, queues, broadcasting Supervisor Keeps queue workers, Octane, Horizon and Reverb running Deployer Atomic, zero-downtime releases (checksum-verified install) Certbot Let's Encrypt certificates and renewals UFW + Fail2ban Firewall and brute-force bans unattended-upgrades Automatic security patches cipi The CLI that ties it all together

Every app is a separate Linux user. If one app is compromised, the others' files, database and processes are out of reach. Area What the app gets Isolation Its own Linux user (home 750 ), PHP pool or Octane process, SSH deploy key Web An Nginx vhost tuned for Laravel; aliases, redirects, basic auth PHP Version per app, changeable any time; php.ini via cipi ini Data Its own database and user (MariaDB or PostgreSQL); its own Valkey instance Processes Queue workers or Horizon, scheduler, optional Reverb Deploys Zero-downtime releases, last 5 kept, one-command rollback TLS Let's Encrypt, HTTP or Cloudflare DNS validation, wildcards Safety nets Health check after each deploy with automatic rollback, backups, monitoring Laravel is the default app type. --node builds and serves a React, Vue, Next.js, Nuxt or Astro frontend; --custom hosts WordPress or plain PHP without database or workers.

If permissions get mangled (an archive unpacked as root, a chmod 775 .ssh ), cipi app fix-permissions myapp restores them. Do not chown -R : Nginx writes logs as www-data and SSH refuses a deploy key with loose permissions.

d: Run apps on FrankenPHP, convert existing apps and pin builds.
x: Laravel Octane keeps your app booted in memory and serves requests with FrankenPHP. Typical result: much lower response times for the same hardware. Octane and PHP-FPM apps run side by side on one server. $ cipi app create shop --octane $ cipi app convert legacy --to=octane $ cipi frankenphp upgrade --all Create or convert Your repository needs laravel/octane , installed with php artisan octane:install --server=frankenphp . Octane starts after the first deploy. cipi app create --user=myapp --domain=myapp.com \ --repository=git@github.com:you/myapp.git --octane cipi app convert myapp --to=octan

Your repository needs laravel/octane , installed with php artisan octane:install --server=frankenphp . Octane starts after the first deploy. cipi app create --user=myapp --domain=myapp.com \ --repository=git@github.com:you/myapp.git --octane cipi app convert myapp --to=octane # an existing FPM app cipi app convert myapp --to=fpm # and back cipi app limits myapp --octane-workers=4

Nginx static files, proxy to Octane Octane on 127.0.0.1 port 8100–8999 FrankenPHP build pinned per app Supervisor keeps it running, reloads on deploy Step 1 of 4 Nginx Nginx terminates HTTPS and serves files in public/ directly (CSS, JS, images). Everything else goes to Octane. Step 2 of 4 Octane on 127.0.0.1 Octane listens on 127.0.0.1 on a port Cipi picks between 8100 and 8999. It's never reachable from the internet directly. Step 3 of 4 FrankenPHP build Each Octane app uses its own FrankenPHP binary, pinned so a deploy never changes the PHP version by surprise. Step 4 of 4 Supervisor Supervisor keeps Octane running, restarts it if it crashes, and reloads it on every deploy. Previous Next step Piece Setting Nginx proxy_pass to the app's local port; static files from current/public ; no PHP-FPM pool Process Supervisor program myapp-octane , next to the queue workers Deploys The pinned FrankenPHP binary is linked into each release, then Octane reloads .env OCTANE_SERVER=frankenphp , OCTANE_HTTPS=true Converting rewrites the vhost, process, deploy recipe and .env , and keeps the certificate. It turns JIT off; enable it again if you use it.

The PHP an Octane app runs is the one compiled into its FrankenPHP binary. Cipi keeps those binaries in /opt/cipi-frankenphp/builds/ (read-only to apps) and pins one per app . A deploy never downloads a new binary, so PHP changes only when you decide. cipi frankenphp # each app's build and PHP, patched or not cipi frankenphp upgrade myapp # newest build on the same PHP minor cipi frankenphp upgrade --all cipi frankenphp use myapp # pin a specific build cipi frankenphp import ./frankenphp # a build you compiled (other PHP minor) cipi frankenphp adopt myapp # pin the binary Octane downloaded cipi frankenphp prune # remove unused builds Rule Why it keeps you stable Upgrades stay on the app's PHP minor and FrankenPHP major No surprise PHP 8.5 → 8.6 jump Octane must answer after an upgrade, or the previous build returns A bad build never stays live A deploy that needs a newer FrankenPHP stops before migrations The live release is untouched; run cipi frankenphp upgrade Apps on different PHP minors use different builds 8.5 and 8.6 coexist Nightly patches via cipi autoupdate (component frankenphp ) Security fixes without manual work To move an app to a new PHP minor: cipi app edit myapp --php=8.6 , then cipi frankenphp upgrade myapp . Octane serves HTTP only. Run long jobs on queue workers or Horizon and WebSockets on Reverb .
Problem Fix 502 after converting Octane not running: cipi worker list myapp , logs with --type=worker Users see others' data A state leak in long-lived objects: see the Octane guide

d: Turn the OPcache JIT on or off for a single app.
x: PHP's JIT compiles hot code to machine code. It helps CPU-bound work (calculations, big collections, heavy templating) and does little for requests that mostly wait on the database. Cipi turns it on for one app , FPM or Octane, and checks it before and after. Commands cipi app jit myapp on # tracing mode, 128M buffer cipi app jit myapp on --mode=function --buffer=256M cipi app jit myapp off cipi app jit myapp --json # current state Safety checks Check When If it fails PHP can start with JIT (no Xdebug/pcov, JIT compiled in) Before Refused, nothing written PHP-FPM active / Octane answering Afte
cipi app jit myapp on # tracing mode, 128M buffer cipi app jit myapp on --mode=function --buffer=256M cipi app jit myapp off cipi app jit myapp --json # current state
Check When If it fails PHP can start with JIT (no Xdebug/pcov, JIT compiled in) Before Refused, nothing written PHP-FPM active / Octane answering After Previous setting restored

Runtime Where the setting goes Side effect PHP-FPM The app's pool, plus a small server-wide file that makes JIT startable for that PHP version Restarts that version's PHP-FPM (all its apps, briefly) Octane The app's own ini directory Restarts only that app's Octane A value forced with cipi ini wins. cipi app convert resets JIT. d: SPA, static and SSR frontends built on every deploy.
x: Node apps build and serve modern front-ends with the same lifecycle as Laravel apps: releases, rollback, webhook, SSL, basic auth, redirects, proxies and the deploy audit. # Vite SPA: build, serve dist/ with an index.html fallback cipi app create --user=web --domain=web.example.com \ --repository=git@github.com:you/web.git --node=spa --framework=vite # Pre-rendered site (Astro, Nuxt generate, Next export) cipi app create --user=docs --domain=docs.example.com \ --repository=git@github.com:you/docs.git --node=static --output=dist # Node server with blue/green deploys cipi app create --user=shop

Mode Nginx Use for spa Serves the build; unknown paths fall back to /index.html Client-side routed apps static Serves the build; real 404s via /404.html Pre-rendered sites ssr Proxies to a Node process on localhost, WebSockets included Next.js, Nuxt, SvelteKit, Remix, Astro SSR Hashed assets ( assets/ , _astro/ , _nuxt/ , _app/immutable/ ) are cached as immutable; HTML is never cached.

Flag Meaning --framework Preset: vite (spa), next , nuxt , sveltekit , astro , remix (ssr). Explicit flags win --node-version LTS major: 22 or 24 (default: the server default ) --build Build command (default npm run build ) --start SSR start command, a Node runner plus arguments, e.g. node build --output Build folder for spa/static; the deploy fails if it has no index.html --health-path SSR path that must answer below 500 before a release takes traffic (default / ) The build installs from your lockfile ( npm ci , pnpm install --frozen-lockfile , yarn install --immutable , bun install --frozen-lockfile ) with NODE_ENV=production . shared/.env is read at build time and by SSR servers at runtime; edit it with cipi app env .

Start new release on the idle slot Health check must answer < 500 in 60 s Switch upstream nginx -t, reload Drain old slot then stop it Step 1 of 4 Start new release Each Node app has two slots (blue and green). The new release starts on the slot that isn't serving traffic. Step 2 of 4 Health check It must answer with a status below 500 within 60 seconds. If it crashes or never answers, it's stopped and the deploy fails: visitors never see it. Step 3 of 4 Switch upstream Nginx is pointed at the new slot, tested with nginx -t , and reloaded gracefully. Step 4 of 4 Drain old slot The old slot finishes its open requests, then stops. Rollback switches back the same way. Previous Next step Two Supervisor programs ( shop-node-blue , shop-node-green ) each own a local port. If the new release crashes or never answers, it is stopped, the old slot keeps serving and the deploy fails before anything goes live. Rollback and cipi node restart switch the same way. The switch runs as root through a narrow rule: ports, start command, Node version and health path come from a root-owned file, not from the app. .env is read as data, never executed; HOST is forced to 127.0.0.1 and the start command runs without a shell.

cipi node status shop # mode, commands, slots cipi node restart shop # zero downtime cipi node logs shop --lines=100 cipi app edit shop --start="node .output/server/index.mjs" --health-path=/health cipi app edit web --node=static --output=dist The same settings can live in your repository in the node: section of cipi.yml . Push-to-deploy works without a Laravel agent: Cipi ships a hardened webhook receiver that verifies GitHub/Bitbucket signatures and GitLab/Azure tokens. Node apps get no database by default; add one with cipi db . cipi sync and cipi app clone do not handle Node apps yet.

d: Push to deploy with the agent, or deploy from your pipeline: how each works and which to pick.
x: A Cipi deploy always runs on your server , as the app's own Linux user. The server pulls the code from Git, builds a new release next to the live one and switches to it in one step. Nothing is uploaded from your laptop or your CI, and no build artifacts travel over the network. What changes from one setup to another is only who says "deploy now" . There are two main ways to say it, plus a few manual ones: Push to deploy (agent mode) Pipeline mode In one sentence Every push to the deploy branch goes live by itself Your CI decides when to deploy, usually after the tests pass Who starts the deplo

From here on, all of them take exactly the same path. Step 2 of 6 Lock Cipi takes the app's deploy lock. If another deploy is already running, the new one waits or stops with a clear "locked" message: two deploys never write the same release. Step 3 of 6 Build release A new folder under releases/ gets the code of the deploy branch, its Composer packages and, if you set a build command, its front-end assets. The live site is not touched yet: if anything fails here, nothing is published and the previous release keeps serving. Step 4 of 6 Migrate Migrations run against the live database. If you turned on pre-deploy snapshots , Cipi takes one just before, as a restore point. Step 5 of 6 Swap The current link moves to the new release in a single operation. Visitors go from the old code to the new one without a single failed request. Step 6 of 6 Verify Workers and Horizon restart on the new code, the health check calls your app (if you set one) and the notification goes out. With automatic rollback on, an unhealthy release is replaced by the previous one within seconds. h: Push to deploy: the agent mode
x: The simplest setup, and the right one for most apps. You push, the app is live about a minute later. git push to the deploy branch Webhook signed HTTPS call to the app Agent checks it signature and branch Server deploys within a minute Step 1 of 4 git push You push to the app's branch ( main by default). Pushes to other branches are answered and ignored. Step 2 of 4 Webhook GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Gitea, Forgejo or Azure DevOps call https://your-app/cipi/webhook . The request is signed with a secret only your server and the provider know. Step 3 of 4 Agent checks it In a Laravel app, the cipi/agent package checks the signature and the branch, writes a small trigger file and answers 200 immediately. It never runs the deploy inside a web request. Step 4 of 4 Server deploys A cron job on the server finds the trigger and starts the normal deploy as the app user. Previous Next step Why it is built this way: No server access for anyone. The provider talks to your app over HTTPS, like any visitor. No SSH key leaves the server and no extra port opens. Instant answer, safe deploy. The webhook returns in milliseconds, so providers never time out, and the deploy runs with the same rights as cipi deploy . Set up for you. With a provider token saved ( cipi git github-token … ), Cipi creates the webhook and the secret when you create the app. See Git providers . Node apps don't need the agent: Cipi installs a built-in receiver for them. Full details: Auto-deploy on push .

Your CI runs the tests first and asks for a deploy only if they pass. The server still does the deploy itself: the pipeline only gives the order, in one of three ways. The webhook only queues the deploy and answers at once. Stop workers no old code on new data Clone into releases/N Composer --no-dev, app's PHP Link shared .env, storage Migrate & optimize migrate --force, optimize Swap current → releases/N Restart & verify workers, health check Step 1 of 7 Stop workers Queue workers stop first (each finishes its current job), so no job runs old code against a database the new release is about to migrate. Step 2 of 7 Clone The repository is cloned into a new folder, releases/<timestamp> . The live release is untouched and keeps serving visitors. Step 3 of 7 Composer composer install --no-dev runs with the app's PHP version, inside the new folder. Step 4 of 7 Link shared .env and storage/ live in shared/ and are linked into the release, so they survive every deploy and rollback. Step 5 of 7 Migrate & optimize php artisan migrate --force and optimize run in the new release. If something fails here, the deploy stops and the old release is still live. Step 6 of 7 Swap The current link switches to the new folder in one atomic step. Requests before the switch got the old code; requests after get the new one. None fail. Step 7 of 7 Restart & verify Workers start again on the new code. With a health check set, Cipi probes the site and can roll back automatically. Previous Next step Deployer and Composer always use the app's PHP version , whatever started the deploy. Old releases beyond the last five are pruned. Octane apps reload Octane; apps with a front-end build run it before the swap.

(safe to poll) cipi deploy myapp --history Past deploys and rollbacks: result, release, duration, trigger cipi deploy --last The last deploy of every app cipi deploy myapp --releases Releases on disk with date, duration, commit cipi deploy myapp --log=200 Timestamped deploy log cipi deploy myapp --audit Who deployed what, from where ( audit ledger ) cipi deploy myapp --snapshot Dump the database first ( safe deploy ) cipi deploy myapp --rollback-on-unhealthy Undo the release if the health check fails cipi deploy myapp --key / --webhook Show the deploy key / webhook URL and token cipi deploy myapp --unlock Clear the lock of an interrupted deploy cipi deploy myapp --trust-host=git.example.com:2222 Trust a self-hosted Git server

d: The signed webhook that deploys when you push.
x: Push to your branch and the app is live a minute later. The Git provider calls a signed webhook on your app; the deploy itself runs on the server as the app user. Pushes to other branches are acknowledged and ignored. Step 2 of 5 Provider → /cipi/webhook GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Gitea or Azure DevOps call the app's webhook URL over HTTPS, signed with the app's secret. Step 3 of 5 Verify & queue Cipi checks the signature and the branch. If both are right it leaves a small trigger and answers 200 immediately, so the provider never times out. Step 4 of 5 Cron, within a minute A cron job checks for triggers every minute and starts the deploy as the app's own Linux user, never as root. Step 5 of 5 Deploy From here it's a normal deploy: new release, Composer, migrations, atomic swap, workers restarted. You get the usual notification. Previous Next step The webhook only drops a trigger file; it never runs the deploy itself. That keeps the HTTP answer instant (providers time out after ~10 s) and the deploy in the same safe context as cipi deploy . Receiver Used by Verifies Cipi Agent ( cipi/agent ) Laravel apps GitHub/Bitbucket HMAC, GitLab/Azure token, Gitea/Forgejo signature Built-in receiver Node apps GitHub/Bitbucket HMAC, GitLab/Azure token

x: The agent's webhook also accepts the secret as a Bearer token, so anything that can send an HTTP request can queue a deploy: a CI job, a scheduler, a chat bot. curl -fsS -X POST https://myapp.com/cipi/webhook \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $CIPI_WEBHOOK_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"ref":"refs/heads/main","pusher":{"name":"release-bot"}}' {"status":"queued","app":"myapp","provider":"webhook","branch":"main", …} It queues the deploy and answers at once; it doesn't wait for the result. d: GitHub Actions, GitLab, Bitbucket, Azure, Forgejo, CircleCI and Envoy recipes, over SSH or the API.
x: Pipeline mode lets your CI decide when an app goes live: usually right after the tests pass, sometimes after a backup or a manual approval. The server still does the deploy itself, exactly as with cipi deploy . Your pipeline only gives the order and reads the result. This page has everything you need: how to connect CI to the server safely, a deploy command that never makes things worse, and ready-to-copy recipes for every popular CI. Push to the branch Test php artisan test Deploy SSH or API → cipi deploy Check health URL answers 200 Roll back only if the check fails Step 1 of 5 Push You push to main (or merge a pull request). The pipeline starts. Step 2 of 5 Test The pipeline installs the dependencies and runs your tests on its own machines. If a test fails, it stops here and nothing reaches the server. Step 3 of 5 Deploy The pipeline asks the server to deploy. The server pulls the latest commit of the branch from Git, builds the release and switches to it. The pipeline waits for the answer. Step 4 of 5 Check The pipeline calls a health URL of the app (for example Laravel's /up ). If it answers, the job is green. Step 5 of 5 Roll back If the new release is live but the app doesn't answer, the pipeline rolls back to the previous release and turns red, so you notice. Previous Next step Don't roll back when the deploy command fails. When cipi deploy fails while building the release (Composer, assets, migrations), nothing is published and the previous release is still serving. Rolling back at that point would go one release further back, to older code. Roll back only when the deploy succeeded and the health check then fails, as every recipe on this page does.

h: 1. Choose how CI calls the server
x: SSH API ( cipi-cli or curl ) Agent webhook What CI runs ssh cipi@server "sudo cipi deploy shop" cipi-cli prod deploy shop curl -X POST https://shop.example.com/cipi/webhook … What the secret can do Run any cipi command as root (including deleting apps) Only what the token allows: with deploy-manage , deploy, roll back, unlock and read status Only queue a deploy of that one app Waits for the result Yes Yes No: it answers "queued" and the deploy starts within a minute Server needs Port 22 open to CI cipi api installed cipi/agent in the app (Laravel) Choose it when You want the quickest setup on one server You want the least privilege, or several servers Your tool can only send an HTTP request Our recommendation: the API for production. A leaked API token with only deploy-manage can redeploy your app; a leaked SSH key for the cipi user can do anything Cipi can do.

Every recipe uses the same names, so you can copy them as they are. Secret What it is How to get it SERVER_HOST The server's IP or hostname Your provider's dashboard SERVER_SSH_KEY A private key used only by CI ssh-keygen below SERVER_KNOWN_HOSTS The server's public host key, so CI knows it's talking to your server ssh-keyscan below CIPI_API_URL Your API address, e.g. https://api.example.com cipi api status CIPI_API_TOKEN A token with only deploy-manage cipi api token create below CIPI_WEBHOOK_TOKEN The app's webhook secret cipi deploy shop --webhook HEALTH_URL A URL that answers 200 when the app works, e.g. https://shop.example.com/up Your app ( health checks )

Create a new key on your laptop. Never reuse your personal key or the app's deploy key. ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "ci-deploy" -f ./ci_deploy -N "" cat ./ci_deploy.pub # 1. copy this line ssh cipi@your-server "sudo cipi ssh add '<paste the line>'" # 2. authorize it on the server cat ./ci_deploy # 3. paste the whole file into the CI secret SERVER_SSH_KEY rm ./ci_deploy ./ci_deploy.pub # 4. delete the local copies Then save the server's host key. Run this from a machine that has already connected to the server, and check that the fingerprint matches the one the server shows: ssh-keyscan -t ed25519 your-server # → the CI secret SERVER_KNOWN_HOSTS ssh-keyscan -t ed25519 your-server | ssh-keygen -lf - # on the server, the same fingerprint must appear: ssh-keygen -lf /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key.pub Running ssh-keyscan inside the pipeline on every build works, but it trusts whatever answers on that address. A saved SERVER_KNOWN_HOSTS is what stops a pipeline from sending your deploy to an impostor.

# on the server, once cipi api token create --name=ci-shop --abilities=deploy-manage --expires=2027-12-31 The token is shown once: save it as CIPI_API_TOKEN . If you restrict the API by IP ( cipi api ip-whitelist ), remember that hosted runners (GitHub, GitLab.com, Bitbucket) change IP on every build: allow their published ranges or use a self-hosted runner with a fixed IP.

If the app also deploys on push, every push would deploy twice: once from the webhook, once from the pipeline, and the second one hits the deploy lock and fails. Provider Where GitHub Repository → Settings → Webhooks → the /cipi/webhook hook → untick Active GitLab Project → Settings → Webhooks → delete the /cipi/webhook hook Bitbucket Repository → Repository settings → Webhooks → delete or disable it Gitea / Forgejo Repository → Settings → Webhooks → untick Active Azure DevOps Project settings → Service hooks → disable the Cipi hook cipi git refresh and cipi app webhook recreate create the webhook again. If you run them later, turn it off again.

Every recipe below runs one of these, depending on how CI calls the server. Over SSH , everything runs on the server in one command: ssh cipi@$SERVER_HOST "sudo cipi deploy shop && \ { curl -fsS --retry 5 --retry-delay 5 --retry-all-errors https://shop.example.com/up >/dev/null \ || { sudo cipi deploy shop --rollback; exit 1; }; }" Part What it does sudo cipi deploy shop Builds and publishes the new release. If it fails, the command stops here: nothing was published, and the job fails && { curl … /up Only if the deploy succeeded: calls the app up to 6 times, 5 seconds apart || { sudo cipi deploy shop --rollback; exit 1; } Only if the app doesn't answer: goes back to the previous release and fails the job Over the API , with cipi-cli: cipi-cli profiles add prod --endpoint "$CIPI_API_URL" --token "$CIPI_API_TOKEN" cipi-cli prod deploy shop curl -fsS --retry 5 --retry-delay 5 --retry-all-errors "$HEALTH_URL" >/dev/null \ || { cipi-cli prod deploy rollback shop -y; exit 1; } cipi-cli deploy waits for the deploy and exits with an error if it fails. It waits about nine minutes at most: for longer builds, follow the deploy with cipi-cli prod deploy status shop . Already using Cipi's own automatic rollback ( rollback_on_unhealthy: true )? Then keep the curl check, so the job turns red, but drop the CI rollback: Cipi has already rolled back, and a second rollback would go one release too far.

h: Any CI: the API with curl
x: For CIs without a ready recipe, or when you'd rather not install cipi-cli. Needs curl and jq . #!/usr/bin/env bash set -euo pipefail H="Authorization: Bearer $CIPI_API_TOKEN" job=$(curl -fsS -X POST "$CIPI_API_URL/api/apps/shop/deploy" -H "$H" -H "Accept: application/json" | jq -r .job_id) echo "Deploy job $job" status=pending for i in $(seq 1 180); do # up to 15 minutes status=$(curl -fsS "$CIPI_API_URL/api/jobs/$job" -H "$H" -H "Accept: application/json" | jq -r .data.status) || status=unknown case "$status" in completed|failed) break ;; esac sleep 5 done if [ "$status" != completed ]; then echo "Deploy $status"; exit 1 # failed or still running: nothing to roll back fi curl -fsS --retry 5 --retry-delay 5 --retry-all-errors "$HEALTH_URL" >/dev/null || { curl -fsS -X POST "$CIPI_API_URL/api/apps/shop/deploy/rollback" -H "$H" -H "Accept: application/json" echo "Unhealthy: rollback requested"; exit 1 } echo "Deployed and healthy" The deploy answers 202 with a job_id ; GET /api/jobs/{id} returns pending , running , completed or failed (with the output once finished). See the REST API .

When a tool can only send an HTTP request (a chat bot, a scheduler, a low-code platform), call the app's own webhook. It accepts the webhook secret as a Bearer token, queues the deploy and answers immediately. curl -fsS -X POST "https://shop.example.com/cipi/webhook" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $CIPI_WEBHOOK_TOKEN" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"ref":"refs/heads/main","after":"'"$COMMIT_SHA"'","pusher":{"name":"ci"}}' # {"status":"queued","app":"shop","provider":"webhook","branch":"main",...} Field Optional? Use ref Yes If set, it must be the app's deploy branch, otherwise the answer is skipped after Yes The commit (7 to 40 hex characters), recorded in the deploy audit pusher.name Yes Who asked, recorded in the audit This path needs the cipi/agent package in a Laravel app. It does not wait for the deploy: the server starts it within a minute, and the result arrives through deploy notifications . Don't put the token in the URL ( ?token= ): URLs end up in logs.

Question Answer Does CI build the app and upload it? No. CI runs the tests; the server pulls the code from Git and builds the release itself. Nothing is uploaded. Which commit goes live? The latest commit of the app's branch when the server builds the release. With one deploy at a time per branch (the concurrency , resource_group and lock settings above), that's the commit your tests checked. Can the CI key do anything else? Over SSH, the cipi user can run any cipi command as root, which includes deleting apps. That's why the API with a deploy-manage token is the safer choice for production. Do I need the agent for pipelines? No. SSH and the API work for every app. The agent is only needed for the webhook path. How are migrations run? By the deploy, on the server, inside the new release and before it goes live. CI doesn't run them. Can I require an approval before production? Yes, with your CI's environments: GitHub required reviewers , GitLab protected environments , Azure approvals , Jenkins input .

If the deploy itself fails, nothing was published and nothing is rolled back. Why . The sh '''…''' blocks use single quotes on purpose: the shell, not Groovy, reads $APP and the credentials. d: Let CodeDeploy orchestrate releases on Cipi servers, on EC2 or anywhere.
x: AWS CodeDeploy can orchestrate releases on Cipi servers: it decides when, on which servers and in which order, and Cipi does the deploy on each server. It fits teams that already manage releases in AWS (CodePipeline, CodeBuild, IAM approvals) or that want to roll a release across several Cipi servers one at a time. Cipi doesn't need CodeDeploy. If you only want "tests pass, then deploy", a CI pipeline is simpler. Use CodeDeploy when AWS is already where your releases are managed. How it fits together CodeDeploy normally copies a bundle of files onto the server. With Cipi, the server already kn

CodeDeploy normally copies a bundle of files onto the server. With Cipi, the server already knows how to fetch and build the app from Git, so the CodeDeploy bundle stays tiny: an appspec.yml and two scripts. CodeDeploy runs the scripts; the scripts call Cipi. Release starts CodePipeline, CI or console Agent picks it up outbound HTTPS only ApplicationStart scripts/deploy.sh → cipi deploy ValidateService scripts/validate.sh Next server one at a time or all at once Step 1 of 5 Release starts A deployment is created: by CodePipeline, by your CI with aws deploy create-deployment , or by hand in the console. Step 2 of 5 Agent picks it up The CodeDeploy agent on the Cipi server polls AWS over HTTPS (port 443, outgoing). No inbound port opens. Step 3 of 5 ApplicationStart CodeDeploy runs scripts/deploy.sh , which runs cipi deploy shop . Cipi pulls the branch from Git, builds the release and switches to it with zero downtime. Step 4 of 5 ValidateService CodeDeploy runs scripts/validate.sh : it calls the health URL and, if the app doesn't answer, rolls back with Cipi and fails the deployment. Step 5 of 5 Next server With several servers in the deployment group, CodeDeploy moves to the next one according to the deployment configuration, and stops if one fails. On EC2 , attach an instance profile that can read the deployment bundles (for example the AWS managed policy for CodeDeploy EC2 instances, plus read access to your S3 bucket). h: 2. Create the application and the deployment group
x: In the CodeDeploy console (or with the AWS CLI): Setting Value Application shop , compute platform EC2/On-premises Deployment group production Targets The tag you gave the server(s), e.g. app=shop Deployment configuration CodeDeployDefault.OneAtATime for several servers, AllAtOnce for one Load balancer Off (Cipi switches releases without downtime on each server) Rollbacks Off : see below Turn CodeDeploy's automatic rollback off. CodeDeploy rolls back by deploying the previous bundle again. With Cipi, that would run cipi deploy again, and Cipi always deploys the latest commit of the branch: you would get the new code a second time, not the old one. The validate.sh script below rolls back with Cipi instead, which really returns to the previous release.

h: 3. The bundle: appspec.yml and two scripts
x: Put these in a codedeploy/ folder in the repository. # codedeploy/appspec.yml version: 0.0 os: linux files: - source: / destination: /opt/codedeploy-cipi/shop hooks: ApplicationStart: - location: scripts/deploy.sh timeout: 1800 ValidateService: - location: scripts/validate.sh timeout: 300 #!/usr/bin/env bash # codedeploy/scripts/deploy.sh: CodeDeploy runs it as root set -euo pipefail /usr/local/bin/cipi deploy shop #!/usr/bin/env bash # codedeploy/scripts/validate.sh: health check, Cipi rollback if the app is down set -uo pipefail APP=shop HEALTH_URL=https://shop.example.com/up if ! curl -fsS --retry 5 --retry-delay 5 --retry-all-errors "$HEALTH_URL" >/dev/null; then echo "Unhealthy: rolling back with Cipi" /usr/local/bin/cipi deploy "$APP" --rollback exit 1 fi # Revisions from GitHub carry the commit CodeDeploy was asked to release. if [ -n "${BUNDLE_COMMIT:-}" ]; then live=$(sudo -u "$APP" git -C "/home/$APP/current" rev-parse HEAD 2>/dev/null || true) [ "$live" = "$BUNDLE_COMMIT" ] || echo "Note: live commit $live, requested $BUNDLE_COMMIT (a newer push reached the branch)" fi echo "Healthy" Make both scripts executable before committing: chmod +x codedeploy/scripts/*.sh . Hook Why this one ApplicationStart Runs after CodeDeploy has placed the bundle; it's where the app "starts", so it's where Cipi deploys ValidateService CodeDeploy's place for "is it working?". A non-zero exit fails the deployment and stops it before the next server If the deploy fails while building the release, deploy.sh fails, nothing was published, and validate.sh never runs: there's nothing to roll

From the console ( Create deployment ), from CodePipeline, or from any CI with the AWS CLI. From an S3 bundle (works with any Git host): aws deploy push --application-name shop \ --s3-location s3://my-deploy-bundles/shop/$COMMIT_SHA.zip --source codedeploy aws deploy create-deployment --application-name shop --deployment-group-name production \ --s3-location bucket=my-deploy-bundles,key=shop/$COMMIT_SHA.zip,bundleType=zip From GitHub (after connecting CodeDeploy to GitHub in the console). Note that CodeDeploy then uses the whole repository as the bundle: keep appspec.yml at the repository root in this case, with the paths of the scripts changed to match. aws deploy create-deployment --application-name shop --deployment-group-name production \ --github-location repository=you/shop,commitId=$COMMIT_SHA To wait for the result in CI: aws deploy wait deployment-successful --deployment-id <id> .
If the app also deploys on push, every push would deploy before CodeDeploy does. Turn the /cipi/webhook hook off in your Git provider. Where: CI/CD pipelines .

A typical pipeline: Source (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket or CodeCommit) → Build (CodeBuild runs php artisan test and outputs the codedeploy/ folder as the artifact) → Deploy (CodeDeploy, deployment group production ). Add a Manual approval action before Deploy for production.

h: Staging and production from one repository
x: Each app has an environment label ( production by default; set with --env on create, clone or edit). An app reads cipi-<env>.yml first and falls back to cipi.yml . File Read by Typically cipi-staging.yml apps with --env=staging deploy: { branch: develop } cipi.yml (or cipi-production.yml ) production apps deploy: { branch: main } cipi app clone shop --domain=staging.shop.com --name=shop-stg --env=staging cipi yml plan shop-stg # deploy branch: main → develop (from the next deploy) The server decides which file an app reads, never the file itself: a commit cannot point production at the staging file. h: Why it is safe to accept over Git
x: Anyone who can push controls the file, so it is fail-closed: Guard Effect Configure only It can never create, rename or delete an app Namespaced Databases and backup profiles must belong to the app Own domains only The health check can't aim the server at internal addresses No shell Only allowlisted runners; unknown keys are errors Small YAML subset Anchors, aliases, tags, merges and block scalars are refused Strict proxies Cipi's own ports, link-local and cloud-metadata addresses are refused Server-only settings Disk limit and which environment file is read can't be changed from the file With auto-apply on, push access to the repository means control over this app's configuration. d: A live copy of the app for every pull request, from your laptop, GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket or Jenkins.
x: A preview environment is a live copy of your app for one branch : its own URL with HTTPS, its own database, its own workers. You open a pull request, a link appears; you push again, the preview updates; you merge or close it, the preview disappears with its data. For Cipi, a preview is simply one more app on a server , created and deleted by a short script. No special mode, no container platform: the same isolation, deploys and rollback as production. Commit this as .cipi/preview.sh and make it executable ( chmod +x .cipi/preview.sh ). It runs on your laptop or in CI, needs cipi-cli and git , and talks to the preview server through the API. #!/usr/bin/env bash # .cipi/preview.sh: create, update or delete the preview of one branch. # .cipi/preview.sh up [branch] create it, or update it (PREVIEW_MODE=deploy) # .cipi/preview.sh down [branch] delete it with its database # .cipi/preview.sh url [branch] print its address # .cipi/preview.sh name [branch] print its app name (pv…) # Settings (environment variables): # PREVIEW_DOMAIN required, e.g. preview.example.com # PREVIEW_REPOSITORY SSH clone URL; default: the "origin" remote # PREVIEW_PHP default 8.4 # PREVIEW_MODE webhook (default) or deploy # CIPI_PROFILE cipi-cli profile of the preview server; default "preview" set -euo pipefail ACTION=${1:-up} BRANCH=${2:-$(git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD)} BASE=${PREVIEW_DOMAIN:?Set PREVIEW_DOMAIN, e.g. preview.example.com} PHP=${PREVIEW_PHP:-8.4} MODE=${PREVIEW_MODE:-webhook} PROFILE=${CIPI_PROFILE:-preview} # Cipi needs an SSH clone URL: turn https://host/owner/repo into git@host:owner/repo.git to_ssh() { case "$1" in https://*) local u=${1#https://}; u=${u#*@}; u=${u%.git}; printf 'git@%s:%s.git' "${u%%/*}" "${u#*/}" ;; *) printf '%s' "$1" ;; esac } REPO=$(to_ssh "${PREVIEW_REPOSITORY:-$(git remote get-url origin)}") # Stable names: the same repository and branch always give the same app and address. sha1() { if command -v sha1sum >/dev/null; then sha1sum; else shasum -a 1; fi; } ID=$(printf '%s#%s' "$REPO" "$BRANCH" | sha1 | cut -c

If the preview server has no API, the same steps run over SSH as the cipi user, who may run sudo cipi … without a password. Set PREVIEW_HOST , give CI an SSH key for the cipi user ( how ), and swap each API call of the script for its SSH twin: srv() { ssh cipi@"$PREVIEW_HOST" sudo cipi "$@"; } exists() { srv app show "$APP" >/dev/null 2>&1; } In the script Over SSH cli apps create --user "$APP" … srv app create --user="$APP" --domain="$DOMAIN" --php="$PHP" --repository="$REPO" --branch="$BRANCH" --env=preview cli apps env set "$APP" --set MAIL_MAILER=log srv app env "$APP" --set=MAIL_MAILER=log cli ssl install "$APP" srv ssl install "$APP" cli yml auto "$APP" on -y srv yml auto "$APP" on cli deploy "$APP" srv deploy "$APP" cli apps artisan "$APP" -- db:seed --force srv app artisan "$APP" db:seed --force cli apps delete "$APP" -y srv app delete "$APP" --force The API version gives CI less power (a token limited to what previews need, instead of a key that can run any cipi command): prefer it.

Previews whose branch is gone should go too. This script lists the previews on the server and deletes those whose branch no longer exists in the repository. Run it nightly from any CI scheduler (GitHub schedule , GitLab pipeline schedules, Bitbucket schedules, Jenkins cron ) or from your laptop. #!/usr/bin/env bash # .cipi/preview-cleanup.sh: delete previews whose branch no longer exists set -euo pipefail PROFILE=${CIPI_PROFILE:-preview} REPO=${PREVIEW_REPOSITORY:?set PREVIEW_REPOSITORY to the SSH clone URL} heads=$(git ls-remote --heads origin) # fails, and stops the script, if Git can't be reached cipi-cli "$PROFILE" apps list --json \ | jq -r --arg repo "$REPO" '.data[] | select(.env == "preview" and (.app | startswith("pv")) and .repository == $repo) | "\(.app) \(.branch)"' \ | while read -r app branch; do if grep -q "refs/heads/${branch}$" <<< "$heads"; then echo "keep $app ($branch)" else echo "delete $app ($branch)" cipi-cli "$PROFILE" apps delete "$app" -y fi done It only touches apps that are labelled preview , named pv… and built from this repository, so production apps and other projects' previews are never in its list.

Question Answer Is a preview a real Cipi app? Yes: same isolation, deploys, logs and rollback as production. It's only labelled preview and named pv… . Do previews need a wildcard certificate? No. Each preview gets its own certificate over HTTP; only the DNS record is a wildcard. Can previews run on the production server? Yes, but a separate server keeps reviews from slowing production and keeps the preview token away from production apps. Do tests run before a preview updates? In webhook mode the preview updates on every push, tests or not: that's usually what reviewers want. With PREVIEW_MODE=deploy , put the preview job after your tests. What happens to the database when the preview is deleted? It's deleted with the app, together with the files, the certificate and the deploy key and webhook in the repository. How do I see all previews? cipi-cli preview apps list , or sudo cipi app list on the server: they're the pv… apps. The why and the team workflows: What preview environments can do for your team .

Nginx is excluded from unattended upgrades so it never restarts unexpectedly. Patch it on your terms: cipi nginx upgrade [--yes] # now cipi autoupdate on nginx # or nightly, automatically apt upgrade nginx your nginx.conf kept nginx -t must pass Reload graceful Check binary restart if old workers linger Step 1 of 4 apt upgrade nginx Nginx is upgraded with apt; your nginx.conf and every vhost are kept. Step 2 of 4 nginx -t nginx -t must pass with the new binary before anything reloads. If it fails, the old Nginx keeps running. Step 3 of 4 Reload A graceful reload: new workers start, old ones finish their requests. No connection is dropped. Step 4 of 4 Check binary Cipi checks that the running binary is the new one, and restarts if old workers linger, so the fix is really active. Previous Next step If a long-lived connection (a WebSocket) keeps an old worker on the replaced binary, Cipi restarts Nginx instead of reloading (well under a second of interruption). A server found on Ubuntu's archive Nginx is moved to nginx.org mainline in one simulated-first transaction: if anything can't be done, nothing changes.
cipi nginx default-server status|on|off On by default: requests for unknown hostnames, on HTTP and HTTPS, get an empty reply (444) instead of reaching one of your apps or a tenant resolver.

Cipi generates each vhost ( /etc/nginx/sites-available/myapp ) and regenerates it when you change aliases, PHP, SSL, redirects or proxies. Prefer Cipi's commands and cipi.yml routes over hand edits; if you must edit, test and reload: sudo nano /etc/nginx/sites-available/myapp sudo nginx -t && sudo systemctl reload nginx Hand edits are overwritten by the next regeneration. d: Copy production data without personal data.
x: The anonymizer gives you a copy of production that looks real but contains no real people . Developers, QA, staging and contractors get the same tables, volumes and relations, with e-mails, names, phones, addresses and notes replaced by Faker values. MySQL, MariaDB and PostgreSQL are supported. It lives inside your Laravel app ( cipi/agent ), runs as a queued job, and is safe by construction: the raw dump is deleted as soon as it's processed, outputs are 0600 , database passwords travel in the environment, never on a command line, and the download link expires. Foreign keys and timestamps are never touched. The file is written to ~/.db/anonymization.json with mode 0640 and is never deployed. The API never returns the download URL: the e-mail is the only channel , and it goes only to the email in the request (no CC, no fallback). x: cipi-cli manages your Cipi servers from your laptop, without SSH . It's a single Go binary (Linux and macOS, amd64 and arm64, MIT) that talks to each server's Cipi API : apps, deploys, cipi.yml , SSL, databases and anonymized dumps, PHP, services, keys, SMTP, health checks and disk usage. One profile per server, so a fleet is one command away. $ cipi-cli api token add prod $ cipi-cli status $ cipi-cli staging deploy myapp Each server needs cipi api installed, and a token from cipi api token create . Install chmod +x cipi-cli-* && sudo mv cipi-cli-* /usr/local/bin/cipi-cli # from GitHub Release

chmod +x cipi-cli-* && sudo mv cipi-cli-* /usr/local/bin/cipi-cli # from GitHub Releases cipi-cli version Binaries ship with SHA-256 checksums on GitHub Releases . From source: git clone https://github.com/cipi-sh/cli && cd cli && make build && sudo make install .

A profile is one server: API endpoint plus token, stored in ~/.cipi/config.json (mode 0600 ). cipi-cli api token add prod Cipi API endpoint: https://api.example.com API token: 1|yourtoken... Server profile "prod" saved → ~/.cipi/config.json cipi-cli profiles add staging --endpoint https://api.staging.example.com --token "1|…"

Prefix any command with a profile to target that server, or set a default. cipi-cli prod deploy shop cipi-cli profiles use prod cipi-cli apps list # uses prod cipi-cli staging apps list # an explicit prefix still wins Command Does profiles / profiles list List servers (alias servers ) profiles add <name> Add or update ( --endpoint , --token ) profiles show [name] One profile, token masked, or all profiles use <name> Default server profiles delete <name> Local credentials only; nothing changes on the server

Command Does apps list , apps show <app> List, details (environment included) apps create [flags] Create; prints credentials, deploy key and whether the key can read the repository apps edit <app> [flags] PHP, repository, branch, environment, domain, Node settings apps delete <app> [-y] Delete apps suspend , unsuspend <app> 503 maintenance page, without deleting apps logs <app> [--type --page --per-page] nginx, php, laravel, worker, deploy; page 1 is newest apps artisan <app> <cmd> Artisan as an async job apps run <app> <cmd> Allowlisted binaries ( cipi-cli run-commands ) `apps env show set <app>` Read .env , or --set KEY=VALUE / --unset KEY `apps auth show create update delete <app>` Composer auth.json `apps basicauth status enable disable <app>` HTTP Basic Auth `apps node status restart <app>` Node status, blue/green restart `apps search enable disable <app>` Meilisearch for one app apps webhook recreate <app> [--rotate-secret] New Git webhook, optionally a new secret apps fix-permissions <app> Restore home permissions Create flag Meaning --user , --domain App name (Linux user, database), primary domain --repository , --branch Git source --php e.g. 8.6 --env Environment label; picks cipi-<env>.yml --engine mariadb or pgsql --octane true / frankenphp --node-build Asset build on every deploy, e.g. npm ci && npm run build --custom , --docroot Non-Laravel app --node , --framework , --node-version , --build , --start , --output , --health-path Node apps cipi-cli apps create --user=shop --domain=shop.com --php=8.6 \ --repository=git@github.com:acme/shop.git --branch=main --node

Every primary domain and alias on the server in one table: handy to audit DNS or spot missing certificates. cipi-cli domains DOMAIN APP KIND TYPE PHP SSL shop.com shop primary Laravel 8.6 ✓ www.shop.com shop alias Laravel 8.6 ✓

Command Does deploy <app> Zero-downtime deploy, waits for the job deploy rollback <app> [-y] Previous release deploy unlock <app> Clear a stuck lock `deploy config show set <app>` deploy.php options: --optimize , --storage-link , --queue-restart , --horizon-terminate , --predeploy-snapshot , --node-build , --extra-artisan deploy audit <app> [--days N] Deploy ledger : origin, operator, IP, commit yml <app> The live cipi.yml : file, environment, validity, what applying would change yml apply <app> Apply it as a job `yml auto <app> on off status` Apply after every deploy (asks for confirmation) cipi-cli deploy shop Deploying shop... Polling job #42... completed Deployed to release #14. Zero downtime. yml needs a token with yml-view / yml-manage . With auto-apply on, anyone who can push can change the app's server settings: that's the point, and the reason it asks first.
Command Does ssl install <app> Let's Encrypt for the primary domain and all aliases ssl force <app> Re-apply the HTTP → HTTPS redirect

Command Does www status <app> Current www / apex setup www add <app> Add the counterpart as an alias www force-to-root / force-from-root <app> 301 to apex / to www www clear <app> Remove the canonical redirect

Command Does redirect list <app> Whole-app and path redirects redirect set <app> --to URL [--code] [--keep-path] Whole app to a URL, one hop `redirect enable disable unset <app>` Toggle or remove it redirect add <app> --from /path --to URL Path redirect; a trailing / means prefix redirect remove <app> --from /path Remove `proxies list add remove <app>` Prefix proxies ( --prefix , --upstream , --strip-prefix , --preserve-host , --timeout , --buffering ) cipi-cli redirect add shop --from /blog/ --to https://blog.acme.com/ cipi-cli proxies add shop --prefix /api --upstream http://127.0.0.1:8080 --strip-prefix
cipi-cli aliases add shop www.shop.com cipi-cli aliases list shop cipi-cli aliases remove shop old.shop.com -y cipi-cli ssl install shop # re-issue to cover new aliases

Command Does db engines , db install <engine> Installed engines; install mariadb or pgsql db list [--engine] Databases with sizes db create <name> [--engine] Create db backup <name> Compressed backup on the server db restore <name> [-y] Restore the latest backup db password <name> New password, linked app .env updated db anonymize <app> --email Anonymized dump through cipi/agent db anonymize download <url> [-o file] Download from the signed link ( -o - for stdout)

The CLI reads APP_URL and the anonymizer token from the app's .env through the API and calls the agent on the app. The signed link arrives by e-mail and lasts 15 minutes. cipi-cli apps artisan shop cipi:service anonymize --enable cipi-cli apps artisan shop cipi:generate-token anonymize cipi-cli apps artisan shop cipi:init-anonymize cipi-cli prod db anonymize shop --email dev@example.com ✓ Anonymization job queued for 'shop' cipi-cli db anonymize download "<signed url>" -o - | mysql -u root shop_local Flags: --email , --url (when the app redirects, redirects are never followed), --token , -o , --force . Custom and Node apps are refused.

Command Does php list Installed versions, FPM status, default; legacy versions marked php install <version> 8.3 , 8.4 , 8.5 or 8.6 (async job) Switching the default and removing versions stay on the server ( cipi php switch|remove ).

Command Does services list [name] Status of system services services restart <name> e.g. nginx , mariadb , php8.6-fpm ssh-keys list Authorized keys of the cipi user, with ids ssh-keys add [key] [--file F] Add a public key ssh-keys remove <id> Remove one

d: cipi/sdk for Laravel and any PHP app.
x: cipi/sdk is the PHP client for the Cipi API . From a Laravel app, a Symfony service or a plain script, one token calls the same surface as cipi-cli and the web panel : apps, deploys, cipi.yml , domains, databases, backups and the server. It runs on your machine over HTTPS: no SSH, no shelling out to cipi . composer require cipi/sdk PHP 8.2+ with ext-curl and ext-json ; Laravel optional. Source: github.com/cipi-sh/sdk (MIT). The server needs cipi api and a token with only the abilities this code needs. Client use Cipi\Sdk\Cipi; $cipi = Cipi::connect( baseUrl: 'https://api.example.com', // "/api

use Cipi\Sdk\Cipi; $cipi = Cipi::connect( baseUrl: 'https://api.example.com', // "/api" suffix optional token: getenv('CIPI_TOKEN') ?: '', ); $apps = $cipi->apps()->list(); $job = $cipi->deploys()->start('shop'); // 202 + job_id $done = $cipi->wait($job); // polls until completed or failed Reads return the JSON body as an array; writes return a job you can wait() on. Plain http:// is refused unless you pass ['allow_http' => true] (for a local panel).

Auto-discovered on Laravel 11, 12 and 13. php artisan vendor:publish --tag=cipi-config CIPI_BASE_URL=https://api.example.com CIPI_TOKEN= CIPI_TIMEOUT=30 use Cipi\Sdk\Laravel\Facades\Cipi; Cipi::apps()->list(); Or type-hint Cipi\Sdk\Cipi . The container holds one server; for another, call Cipi::connect() with its URL and token. Symfony and others register Cipi::connect() in their own container. Install it next to cipi/agent and the app's MCP server gains panel tools: panel_rollback , panel_deploy_audit , panel_db_backup , panel_job , panel_status .

$cipi->wait($cipi->apps()->create([ 'user' => 'shop', 'domain' => 'shop.example.com', 'repository' => 'git@github.com:acme/shop.git', 'branch' => 'main', 'php' => '8.6', 'env' => 'production', 'node_build' => 'npm ci && npm run build', ])); $cipi->apps()->update('shop', ['php' => '8.6']); $cipi->apps()->suspend('shop'); $cipi->apps()->unsuspend('shop'); $cipi->apps()->recreateWebhook('shop', rotateSecret: true); $cipi->wait($cipi->limits()->update('shop', ['fpm_max_children' => 10, 'disk_limit_gb' => 5])); $cipi->basicAuth()->enable('shop', 'admin'); $cipi->wait($cipi->artisan()->run('shop', 'migrate --force')); $cipi->wait($cipi->run()->execute('shop', 'composer install --no-dev')); $cipi->logs()->get('shop', 'deploy'); Create accepts the fields of POST /api/apps : user and domain required, plus repository , branch , php , env , custom , octane , engine , node_build , or Node fields. Invalid values throw ValidationException (422). Field Rule env ^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9_-]{0,31}$ , default production ; picks cipi-<env>.yml node_build Starts with npm , npx , yarn , pnpm , bun or node ; && and ; allowed; no pipes, redirects or substitutions; max 200 characters limits() FPM children, memory_limit , Octane workers, queue workers, disk_limit_gb (soft, null removes it) After create (and edits that change repository or branch) the job result carries repository_access : $job = $cipi->wait($cipi->apps()->create($attributes)); $access = $job['data']['result']['repository_access'] ?? null; if ($access && $access['status'] !== 'ok') { // ok, nobranch or denied // $access['error'] is git's lin

$cipi->wait($cipi->deploys()->start('shop')); $cipi->deploys()->rollback('shop'); $cipi->deploys()->unlock('shop'); $cipi->deploys()->audit('shop', days: 30); $cipi->deploys()->status('shop', tail: 50); // running, queued, interrupted, idle $cipi->deploys()->history('shop', limit: 10); $cipi->deploys()->last(); // last run of every app $cipi->deployConfig()->update('shop', ['keep_releases' => 5, 'migrate' => true]); $cipi->jobs()->wait($job, timeoutSeconds: 120, intervalSeconds: 1.0); wait() times out after 300 s by default and throws JobFailedException (payload on $e->job ) when a job fails. $plan = $cipi->yml()->status('shop')['data']; // file, env, valid, in_sync, changes, blockers foreach ($plan['changes'] as $change) { echo $change['summary'], PHP_EOL; // e.g. "PHP 8.5 → 8.6" } if ($plan['blockers'] === []) { $job = $cipi->jobs()->wait($cipi->yml()->apply('shop'), throwOnFailure: false); $outcome = $job['data']['result']['outcome']; // applied, unchanged, partial, blocked, invalid, no-file } $cipi->yml()->enableAuto('shop'); With auto-apply on, anyone who can commit can change the app's aliases, PHP settings, limits, workers, deploy recipe, schedule, databases and backups. Ask for confirmation before enabling it for someone. Reads need yml-view , writes yml-manage .

$cipi->aliases()->add('shop', 'www.shop.example.com'); $cipi->www()->forceToRoot('shop'); $cipi->redirects()->set('shop', 'https://example.com', 301, keepPath: true); $cipi->redirects()->add('shop', '/blog/', 'https://blog.example.com', 301, true); $cipi->proxies()->add('shop', prefix: '/api/', upstream: 'http://127.0.0.1:3000', stripPrefix: true); $cipi->ssl()->install('shop'); $cipi->ssl()->install('shop', dns: 'cloudflare', account: 'prod', wildcard: true); $cipi->ssl()->setDnsAccount($cloudflareToken, 'prod'); // sync, never returned Redirects and proxies are tested with nginx -t and reverted on failure; the proxy loopback guard can't be bypassed. Node apps: node()->status($app) , node()->restart($app) .

$cipi->env()->update('shop', ['APP_ENV' => 'production'], ['TELESCOPE_ENABLED']); // merge, unset $cipi->authJson()->replace('shop', ['http-basic' => ['repo.example.com' => ['username' => 'token', 'password' => $secret]]]); $cipi->wait($cipi->databases()->create('shop_reports', 'pgsql', app: 'shop')); $cipi->databases()->backup('shop'); $cipi->databases()->password('shop'); $cipi->databases()->link('legacy', 'shop'); $cipi->wait($cipi->databases()->restoreLocal('shop', __DIR__.'/shop.sql.gz')); // chunked upload restoreLocal() streams the dump in chunks (not bound by memory_limit ) and cancels the upload if anything is refused. The panel deletes uploads when the restore ends. $cipi->backups()->createProfile('nightly', [ 'scope' => 'all', 'every' => '1d', 'destinations' => ['s3'], 'keep_days' => 14, 'encrypt' => true, ]); $cipi->backups()->status()['data']['uncovered']; // what no enabled profile takes $cipi->backups()->run('nightly'); // starts and returns, not a job $cipi->wait($cipi->backups()->verify('nightly')); Destinations and their keys are configured on the server and never returned.

$cipi->server()->status(); $cipi->php()->install('8.6'); $cipi->ssh()->add($publicKey); $cipi->services()->restart('php8.6-fpm'); $cipi->health()->update('shop', 'https://shop.example.com/up', 200); $cipi->search()->enable('shop'); $cipi->disk()->usage(); $cipi->metrics()->series('shop', ['req', 'http_5xx'], '7d'); // ~240 points of [ts, avg, max] $cipi->metrics()->uptime('shop', '30d'); $cipi->metrics()->setHeartbeat('https://hc-ping.com/<uuid>', every: 1); $cipi->wait($cipi->node()->upgrade(24, restart: true)); $cipi->ipWhitelist()->replace(['203.0.113.10'], ensureClientIp: true); $cipi->request('GET', '/apps/shop'); // any endpoint not wrapped yet Packages, monitor, Zero Trust and disk usage are read-only, as on the API.

Protection Detail Transport HTTPS with verification; redirects never followed, so the token stays on your host Token Only in the Authorization header; whitespace or control characters rejected (no header injection); stripped from exceptions and var_dump Retries Reads may retry 429 / 503 with a short Retry-After ; writes never Limits Responses over 16 MiB refused; 30 s timeout, 10 s connect $cipi = Cipi::connect($url, $token, [ 'timeout' => 30, 'connect_timeout' => 10, 'max_retries' => 2, 'max_response_bytes' => 16777216, 'allow_http' => false, ]); One token per application, smallest ability set, kept in the environment, never committed. A missing ability is a 403, never a silent no-op.

Status Exception 401 AuthenticationException 403 AuthorizationException (missing ability, or IP allowlist) 404 NotFoundException 409 ConflictException 422 ValidationException ( errors() with Laravel's bag) 429 RateLimitException ( retryAfter ) 5xx ServerException none TransportException , ConfigurationException ; from wait() : JobFailedException , TimeoutException try { $cipi->wait($cipi->deploys()->start('shop')); } catch (JobFailedException $e) { $job = $e->job; } catch (AuthorizationException $e) { // token lacks deploy-manage }

d: Create and terminate apps from your billing panel.
x: Sell Laravel and PHP hosting on your own servers. The official WHMCS provisioning module ( github.com/cipi-sh/whmcs , MIT) maps the WHMCS lifecycle to the Cipi API : orders create apps, suspensions take them offline, terminations remove them. A self-contained drop-in, no Composer dependencies. Order paid WHMCS Create Account POST /api/apps isolated app on Cipi Auto-SSL Let's Encrypt (optional) Lifecycle suspend, change package, terminate Step 1 of 4 Order paid A customer pays an order in WHMCS and the product's module runs Create Account. Step 2 of 4 POST /api/apps The module calls the Cipi AP

WHMCS 8.x, a Cipi server with cipi api , and a token with these abilities: Ability For apps-view Test Connection, App Info apps-create Create Account apps-edit Change Package apps-suspend Suspend, Unsuspend apps-delete Terminate deploy-manage Deploy, Rollback, Unlock ssl-manage Install SSL, Auto-SSL

your-whmcs/ └── modules/servers/cipi/ ├── cipi.php └── lib/CipiApiClient.php Copy modules/servers/cipi/ into your WHMCS root. System Settings → Servers → Add New Server : type Cipi (Laravel hosting) , hostname = API base URL (no trailing slash), password = token, Secure = yes. Create a hosting product on that server and set its module settings: Setting Values Default PHP Version 8.3, 8.4, 8.5, 8.6 server default App Type laravel or custom laravel Git Repository (SSH) Required for Laravel, optional for custom — Git Branch Branch to deploy main Auto SSL Certificate right after creation No App type Cipi equivalent Good for laravel cipi app create Laravel apps with Deployer releases, workers, database custom cipi app create --custom WordPress, static sites, SPAs, any PHP; Git optional (SFTP-only hosting)

WHMCS action API call Behaviour Test Connection GET /api/apps Token and reachability Create Account POST /api/apps Provision, wait for the job, optional SSL Suspend POST /api/apps/{name}/suspend 503 maintenance page, nothing deleted Unsuspend POST /api/apps/{name}/unsuspend Normal vhost back Change Package PUT /api/apps/{name} PHP, repository, branch Terminate DELETE /api/apps/{name} Remove the app Admin buttons on the service page: Install SSL , Deploy , Rollback Deploy , Unlock Deploy , App Info . If Auto-SSL fails, the app is still created and a warning is logged. Every call is logged with logModuleCall() (Utilities → Logs → Module Log).

The bundled CipiApiClient covers apps, deploys, SSL, aliases, databases and jobs, for your own hooks: require_once ROOTDIR . '/modules/servers/cipi/lib/CipiApiClient.php'; $client = new CipiApiClient('https://api.example.com', $token); $client->addAlias('myapp', 'alias.example.com'); $client->createDatabase('myapp_extra'); $client->backupDatabase('myapp'); The module adds no client-area tab. One-time secrets Cipi generates (SSH and database passwords, deploy key, webhook) aren't pushed to WHMCS: deliver them with a hook or your support workflow. For richer tooling use the PHP SDK .

d: Forge, Ploi, Vito Deploy, Coolify and others, compared.

The benchmark: built by the Laravel team, polished and battle-tested at huge scale, with multi-cloud provisioning, teams and monitoring. Choose Forge if you want the most mature hosted dashboard and provider integrations. Choose Cipi to stop paying per server, keep management on the server itself (no SaaS to be reachable), version server settings in cipi.yml , script everything from the CLI and drive it from AI assistants. Cipi vs Forge .

A Forge-like SaaS panel from the Netherlands, natively GDPR-friendly, with a clean UI and built-in backups and monitoring. Choose Ploi for a cheaper hosted GUI with EU data handling. Choose Cipi when you want no third party at all, no plan limits, and the CLI, API and MCP surface. Not to be confused with Ploi Cloud . Cipi vs Ploi .

The closest in spirit: free, open source, self-hosted, a GUI built with Laravel, teams and plugins. Vito runs as its own Laravel app with a database, usually on a dedicated VPS; Cipi lives on the server it manages and adds the panel only if you want it. Cipi adds cipi.yml , MCP, an encrypted vault, server sync, a deploy audit trail and automatic security patching. Cipi vs Vito Deploy .

Hosted panels from roughly $8 to $49 per server per month. RunCloud and ServerPilot lean towards WordPress and generic PHP; Cleavr and moss.sh support Laravel through a hosted GUI (moss.sh caps deploys on its free tier). Cipi gives you Laravel-aware automation (Deployer releases, workers, scheduler, Horizon, Reverb, Octane) for nothing. RunCloud · Cleavr · ServerPilot · moss.sh .

Free and polished, for PHP, Node, Python and static sites. A generic multi-stack panel with no Laravel release or worker management. Pick it if Python sites matter to you; pick Cipi for Laravel depth. Cipi vs CloudPanel .

You don't touch a server; you pay for resources and accept the platform's limits. Platform Strength Choose Cipi when Laravel Cloud Autoscaling, scale-to-zero, managed databases and edge, from the Laravel team You want a fixed bill, root and a portable stack Ploi Cloud EU PaaS for Laravel, PHP and Node, memory-based pricing You'd rather own the VPS and pay the provider only Render Multi-language, previews, private networking, compliance options Your apps are Laravel/PHP and you want no usage invoice Sevalla Apps, databases and storage under one managed bill You want native Laravel on your own Ubuntu fortrabbit PHP-specialised managed hosting with a long track record You want root, Octane, Horizon and Reverb under your control

Coolify , Dokku and Easypanel deploy containers on your server, free. Great when you host many stacks and already think in Docker. Cipi runs a native Nginx + PHP-FPM/Octane + MariaDB/PostgreSQL stack with no container layer: less overhead, simpler debugging, and Laravel's lifecycle (releases, workers, scheduler, Horizon, Reverb) built in.

Kamal ships containers over SSH to servers you've already prepared. It doesn't install the web server, PHP, databases, firewall, certificates, backups or workers. Cipi does all of that, and deploys. Choose Kamal if you have Docker infrastructure and need only the deploy step.

cPanel , Plesk and DirectAdmin are built for selling shared hosting: e-mail, FTP, DNS and many customer sites, under a licence. Right for hosting resellers, heavy for a team deploying its own apps. HestiaCP (the maintained fork of the abandoned VestaCP) is a free, lighter alternative for e-mail, DNS and many websites, with no Laravel tooling. aaPanel is a free, plugin-based multi-stack panel popular in Asia-Pacific, GUI-centric, also without Laravel automation. GridPane, xCloud and ServerAvatar focus on WordPress and WooCommerce: staging clones, multisite, WordPress caching. For WordPress fleets, evaluate them on their merits. Cipi runs WordPress as a custom app when it sits next to your Laravel apps. 20i is a hosting company (reseller, WordPress, VPS, domains, e-mail, 24×7 support). It covers a full hosting catalogue; Cipi replaces it only for "deploy my apps on a VPS I own". Cipi vs 20i .

A small VPS is enough for staging. Every production provisioner has the same constraint. What Cipi doesn't ask for is the difference: no agent phoning home, no external control plane, no cloud account. Locally , use Laravel Herd , Sail or php artisan serve , then push to a Cipi server for staging and production.

Cipi installs Nginx, PHP-FPM, MariaDB or PostgreSQL, Valkey and Supervisor as native Ubuntu packages , managed by systemd, and seals apps off from each other with Linux users. There are no containers, no images and no Docker daemon on a Cipi server. That's deliberate: for one server running Laravel and PHP apps, Docker adds a layer that has to be secured, patched and debugged, without giving anything the OS doesn't already provide. Every task goes through Docker first One command per task ( cipi app create , cipi deploy , cipi ssl install ). Underneath, a plain Ubuntu server: nothing to translate An extra layer Docker sits between you and every component: to change a php.ini or an Nginx rule you edit an image or a mount, then recreate The component is the one on the host: /etc/nginx , /etc/php , managed by Cipi and visible to you SSH and SFTP SSH lands on the host, not in the app: then docker exec into a container that usually has no SSH, no editor and no SFTP ssh myapp@server drops you into the app as its own user, with artisan , composer , logs and SFTP for your IDE Remote databases The database lives on a container network. To reach it from TablePlus or DBeaver you publish its port (bypassing the firewall, see below) or chain an SSH tunnel into the container network Native MariaDB or PostgreSQL on localhost: connect over SSH with the mariadb+ssh:// URL shown at creation. Cipi is the Italian reading of the letters C and P : Control Panel . A nod to the project's Italian roots, and to what it does under the hood: manage Nginx, PHP-FPM, databases, Supervisor, certificates and the firewall for you. The mascot is a penguin, a reference to Tux , the Linux mascot drawn by Larry Ewing in 1996. Same species, different attitude: minimal, hand-sketched, happier in the terminal than in the spotlight.

d: From shell scripts in 2019 to Cipi 5.
x: Cipi was created by Andrea Pollastri , a developer since 2005 working on Laravel, system administration and security, with experience at companies like Docebo and Musement. He built it out of a practical need: a fast, scriptable way to put Laravel apps on his own VPS without handing control to a SaaS panel. The private tool became an open-source project with over 1,000 GitHub stars and servers running it around the world. Seven years, five major versions, one idea that never changed: your server, your apps, no bill for the tool. v0.1 June 2019 The idea A handful of shell scripts that set up Ng
A handful of shell scripts that set up Nginx, PHP, MariaDB and Supervisor on a fresh Ubuntu VPS. No UI, no package. Just bash. v1–v2 2019–2020

The scripts were wrapped in a Laravel web panel hosted on the same server: create apps, deploy, configure Nginx from the browser. A year of iteration added SMTP, database backups, service management and dozens of fixes, and Cipi became a stable choice for small-team Laravel hosting. v3 2021

Rebuilt on Laravel 8 with a documented REST API, PHP 8, live CPU and RAM charts, a cron editor, Supervisor and GitHub management. The 3.1 series was the most polished release of the web-UI era, and many teams ran it for years. It also raised the question that shaped what followed: was a browser panel still the right interface, when deploys were moving to SSH, CI pipelines and automation? v4 2026

The web UI was dropped and Cipi became a CLI operated over SSH, with every part of the stack tuned for Laravel. MariaDB replaced MySQL, Deployer brought zero-downtime releases, each app got its own Linux user and deploy key, and GitHub and GitLab webhooks, S3 backups, encrypted server sync, a REST API and MCP servers for AI agents arrived. Late v4 added optional PostgreSQL and the return of a web panel, this time as an optional add-on. v5 2026, today
